title: How AI Adoption Might Affect Bank Lending - San Francisco Fed
gist: SF Fed research finds banks that post more AI-skill job openings earn higher returns on assets but also carry more problem loans and lend less to small and medium enterprises, because current AI tools are better at processing hard credit data than the soft, relationship-based information SME lending relies on.

themes.theme: AI adoption race across bank sizes

insights.claim: The share of AI-related job postings in the U.S. banking sector rose from under 0.94% in 2015 to 6.80% by the end of 2025, a far faster increase than in the broader finance, insurance, and real estate (FIRE) sector (3.20%) or the whole economy (2.69%).
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: Banks are the clearest bellwether for how AI adoption is reshaping a knowledge-intensive industry ahead of the rest of the economy.
insights.quote: the share of AI job postings in the banking industry surged to 6.80% by the end of 2025, up from less than 0.94% in 2015
insights.locator: Figure 1 AI adoption in banking and in other selected sectors

insights.claim: By the end of 2025, large banks (assets over $100 billion) had an 8.86% share of AI-related job postings versus 4.48% for medium-sized banks and only 1.15% for small banks (assets under $10 billion), and 84% of small banks in the sample had never posted an AI-related job.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: AI capability is concentrating scale advantages further at large banks, widening the competitive gap with community and regional lenders.
insights.quote: the share of AI-related job postings by small banks was only 1.15%, far below those for medium-sized banks (4.48%) and for large banks (8.86 %)
insights.locator: Figure 2 AI adoption shares by bank size

insights.claim: Small and medium-sized banks lag in AI adoption because they face financing constraints for AI investment, difficulty attracting AI-skilled workers, limited access to the data needed to train or deploy AI, and reliance on older computing infrastructure poorly suited to AI applications.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: These structural barriers are unlikely to close quickly, implying the AI-driven divergence between large and small banks could persist for years absent third-party AI tools leveling the field.
insights.locator: Small and medium-sized banks face greater hurdles

insights.claim: Current AI and information technologies are primarily effective at processing 'hard information' such as credit scores, financial statements, and formal credit histories, but are much less capable of processing 'soft information' such as personal relationships and local market knowledge.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: This hard-versus-soft information distinction is the core mechanism explaining why AI benefits large-borrower lending more than relationship-based lending, and is a lens investors can apply to other AI-adoption stories in services industries.
insights.locator: Studies suggest that AI and other information technologies primarily help

insights.claim: Because small and medium enterprise (SME) lending relies heavily on soft information like borrower relationships and knowledge of local economic conditions, AI adoption tends to tilt bank lending activity away from SMEs and toward borrowers with more readily digitized hard data.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: As AI adoption spreads, SMEs may face a structurally shrinking pool of bank credit unless GenAI closes the soft-information gap or alternative lenders step in.
insights.quote: Because soft information is harder to process using currently available AI tools, AI adoption might tilt bank lending away from SMEs.
insights.locator: Studies suggest that AI and other information technologies primarily help

themes.theme: AI-driven risk-taking: higher returns, more problem loans

insights.claim: By enabling banks to more easily manage complex loans, AI adoption encourages banks to take on more risk in lending, which requires higher risk compensation and should raise average bank returns on assets.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: AI adoption is a plausible driver of bank profitability dispersion, useful for evaluating why AI-forward banks report stronger margins.
insights.locator: By enhancing how banks gather and process information

insights.claim: Banks with above-average shares of AI-related job postings ('high-AI' banks) had an average return on assets about 0.38 percentage point higher than 'low-AI' banks between 2021 and 2025, and among large banks specifically the ROA gap widened to 0.61 percentage point.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: A quantifiable profitability premium (38-61 bps of ROA) tied to AI intensity gives investors a concrete metric to screen bank stocks on AI adoption proxies like hiring data.
insights.quote: The average ROA for high-AI banks is about 0.38 percentage point higher than for low-AI banks.
insights.locator: Figure 3 AI adoption impact on ROA, problem loan shares

insights.claim: High-AI banks also carry higher average shares of problem loans (those rated substandard or with doubtful repayment) than low-AI banks, though the gap is smaller than the ROA gap, consistent with AI-enabled banks taking on riskier, more complex loans in exchange for higher returns.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: The AI profitability premium comes bundled with credit-quality risk, so investors should weight AI-intensive banks' higher ROA against latent asset-quality risk in a downturn.
insights.locator: Figure 3 shows that increased AI adoption is associated with higher average ROA

insights.claim: The authors caution that the AI-ROA and AI-problem-loan correlations are not necessarily causal, because banks that already hold more complex, risky loan portfolios may have greater incentive to invest in AI to manage those loans, creating reverse causality.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: Investors should treat the AI-adoption-to-profitability link as a correlation to monitor, not a proven causal driver to bet on directly.
insights.quote: we cannot make causal claims here, as banks with greater shares of complex loans in their portfolios would also have more incentives to invest in AI technology
insights.locator: This Economic Letter examines how AI adoption might affect bank lending

themes.theme: SME credit squeeze from AI adoption

insights.claim: In the full sample, high-AI banks directed only about 12% of their loans to small and medium enterprises (SMEs), versus 21% for low-AI banks, and this pattern held across small, medium, and large bank size groups.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: A roughly 9-point gap in SME loan share tied to AI intensity signals a measurable credit-access risk for small business borrowers as bank AI adoption scales up.
insights.quote: high-AI banks have a much smaller average share of SME loans than low-AI banks (12% versus 21%)
insights.locator: Figure 4 Higher use of AI associated with reduced SME lending

insights.claim: The gap in SME loan shares between high-AI and low-AI banks is largest among small banks (13.3% versus 21.4%), narrower among medium-sized banks (3.8% versus 7.8%), and smallest among large banks (2.2% versus 3.3%).
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: The SME lending pullback from AI adoption is most acute exactly where SMEs have traditionally relied most on their banking relationship (small community banks), suggesting the least AI-flexible lenders may be squeezed hardest if forced to compete on AI capability.
insights.locator: The difference in the shares of SME loans between high-AI and low-AI banks is most pronounced

insights.claim: The authors predict that continued growth in bank AI adoption could create more difficulties for SME financing going forward, though they caveat that it is premature to know how AI capabilities will develop and whether AI's current advantage in processing hard information over soft information will persist.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: A structurally tightening SME credit market is a watch item for small-business lenders, fintech alternative lenders, and policymakers, but the authors' own hedging means it should not be treated as a settled forecast.
insights.quote: This may suggest more difficulties for SME financing going forward as AI adoption continues to grow.
insights.locator: Our results therefore suggest that increased AI usage by banks

insights.claim: Generative AI (GenAI) might eventually help banks process soft information as well as hard information, which could narrow or reverse the current AI-driven SME lending gap.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: A future GenAI breakthrough in processing relationship and qualitative data would be a bullish catalyst for SME credit access and for banks currently disadvantaged in hard-data-driven AI lending models.
insights.quote: GenAI might eventually assist banks in processing soft data, which could bridge the information gap for SME lending.
insights.locator: However, the potential impact of AI adoption on SME lending

insights.claim: Because bank-level AI adoption data is not publicly available, the researchers proxy AI usage intensity using the share of a bank's online job postings requiring AI or generative-AI skills, drawn from Lightcast data and FFIEC Call Report filings, covering 1,006 banks representing over 87% of total U.S. banking system assets.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: Investors and researchers can replicate or extend this hiring-based AI-adoption proxy methodology to track AI intensity in other industries where direct adoption data is unavailable.
insights.locator: Since bank-level AI adoption information is not publicly available

insights.claim: The job-postings-based AI adoption measure likely overstates the true disparity in AI usage between small and large banks, because small banks lacking in-house resources may instead access AI through third-party vendors, which would not show up as AI-related hiring.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: The true AI capability gap between small and large banks may be narrower than the headline hiring data suggests, tempering conclusions about how disadvantaged small banks really are.
insights.quote: Thus, our measure may overstate the disparities in AI adoption by bank size.
insights.locator: One caveat of our measure of AI adoption based on online job postings

themes.theme: Banks as an early signal for AI's economy-wide impact

insights.claim: Because commercial banks are among the earliest and most intensive adopters of AI across all sectors of the economy, their observed lending pattern changes may offer an early preview of how AI adoption will affect information processing, risk-taking, and access to credit as AI spreads to other business sectors.
insights.speaker: Greeshma Avaradi
insights.so_what: Investors tracking AI's broader economic impact should treat bank lending data as a leading indicator rather than a banking-sector-only story.
insights.quote: to the extent that commercial banks are industry leaders in AI adoption, their experiences may shed some light on the broader economic impacts of AI as its adoption spreads to other business sectors
